unmatched_peer.body: If the pending task (e.g. `run_get_response`) raises an exception other than `CancelledError` after being cancelled, that exception is silently swallowed here. The `await pending` after `pending.cancel()` will re-raise whatever the task raised — if the view raised a `ValueError`, `TypeError`, or any other unhandled exception, it would be lost. Only `CancelledError` is expected here; any other exception should propagate.
unmatched_peer.rationale: When `pending.cancel()` is called on `run_get_response`, the task may have already completed with an exception before the cancel was processed. In that case `await pending` re-raises the original exception, not `CancelledError`. The bare `except asyncio.CancelledError: pass` will not catch it, but there is no other handler, so it would propagate up and bypass the `body_file.close()` cleanup below.

unmatched_peer.body: `body_file` is not closed when `done.result()` raises an exception that is neither `RequestAborted` nor `AssertionError`. For example, if `run_get_response` raises an unexpected exception (e.g. an unhandled view exception that somehow escapes), `body_file` will be leaked. Consider using a `finally` block or a context manager to ensure `body_file.close()` is always called.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The existing `read_body` path already closes `body_file` on `RequestAborted`, but the new concurrent-task path only closes it in the two explicit `except` branches. Any other exception from `done.result()` will skip both `body_file.close()` calls.

unmatched_peer.body: The unpacking `done, pending = done.pop(), pending.pop()` assumes exactly one task in each set. While `asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED` with two tasks guarantees at least one done and at most one pending, if both tasks complete simultaneously (a race condition), `done` could contain two items and `pending` would be empty — causing `pending.pop()` to raise `KeyError`.
unmatched_peer.rationale: With `asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED`, if both tasks finish in the same event-loop iteration, both end up in `done` and `pending` is empty. This is a real (if rare) scenario, e.g. when `listen_for_disconnect` and `run_get_response` both complete before the event loop yields. The `pending.pop()` would then raise `KeyError`.

unmatched_peer.body: `hello_with_delay` uses `time.sleep(1)` (a blocking synchronous sleep) inside what is used as a delayed ASGI view. Under ASGI, this blocks the event loop for 1 second, which is both slow and incorrect for async testing. It should use `asyncio.sleep` (and be an `async def`) to properly yield control to the event loop during the delay.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `test_delayed_disconnect_with_body` test uses this view via the `/delayed_hello/` URL. Since ASGI runs on an event loop, a blocking `time.sleep(1)` will stall the entire event loop, preventing the disconnect message from being processed concurrently. This makes the test unreliable and slow.

unmatched_peer.body: The documentation states that `asyncio.CancelledError` will be raised "in the view", but this only applies to async views. Synchronous views running under ASGI (via `sync_to_async`) will not receive `CancelledError` in the same way. The docs should clarify that this behaviour applies to async views only.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `run_get_response` method calls `get_response_async`, which wraps sync views in `sync_to_async`. A sync view running in a thread pool will not have `CancelledError` propagated into it — the cancellation happens at the asyncio task level, not inside the thread. The docs should note this limitation.

unmatched_peer.body:
When `process_request` (tasks[1]) raises an unexpected exception other than `RequestAborted` or `AssertionError`, it is silently swallowed. The `task.result()` call will re-raise the exception, but only `RequestAborted` and `AssertionError` are caught — any other exception (e.g. an unhandled error from the view or `send_response`) will propagate up and skip the `body_file.close()` on line 224, leaking the temporary file. The old code had the same gap for `AssertionError` (it closed and re-raised), but now any other exception also bypasses the close.

Consider wrapping the entire `for` loop in a `try/finally` that calls `body_file.close()`, or use a context manager for `body_file` throughout `handle()`.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `body_file.close()` on line 224 is only reached if no exception escapes the loop. If `task.result()` raises anything other than `RequestAborted` or `AssertionError`, execution leaves the loop immediately and `body_file` is never closed. The `AssertionError` branch explicitly closes and re-raises, but no other exception type does. This was flagged as a ResourceWarning concern in the prior review discussion (see @felixxm's comments about `SpooledTemporaryFile` leaks).

unmatched_peer.body:
When a pending task is cancelled and `await task` raises something other than `asyncio.CancelledError` (e.g. the view catches `CancelledError` and raises a different exception, or `send_response` raises an I/O error), that exception propagates out of the loop and `body_file.close()` on line 224 is never reached, leaking the temporary file.

The documentation example in `docs/ref/request-response.txt` shows a streaming generator that catches `CancelledError` and re-raises it, which is the expected pattern — but if a view does not re-raise, the task will complete normally (not via `CancelledError`) and the `except asyncio.CancelledError` block won't fire. In that case the code path is actually fine (the task ends up `done()` on the next loop iteration... wait, no — the loop only iterates once per task). Actually if the view swallows `CancelledError`, `await task` returns normally without raising, which is also fine. The real risk is a non-`CancelledError` exception from the task.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `await task` after `task.cancel()` can raise any exception the task raises. Only `asyncio.CancelledError` is caught. Any other exception bypasses `body_file.close()`.

unmatched_peer.body:
The ordering of tasks in the list matters for correctness: the comment says `listen_for_disconnect` goes first so that its errors don't prevent cancellation of `process_request`. However, if `listen_for_disconnect` is done and raises `AssertionError`, the loop raises immediately (after closing `body_file`) without ever cancelling `process_request` (tasks[1]). This leaves `process_request` as an unfinished, uncancelled background task that will continue running (and potentially writing to the already-closed `send` channel) after `handle()` returns.

The `AssertionError` branch should cancel remaining tasks before re-raising.
unmatched_peer.rationale: In the loop, when `task.done()` is True and `task.result()` raises `AssertionError`, the code does `body_file.close(); raise`. At that point `tasks[1]` (process_request) may still be pending and is never cancelled. The old code always cancelled the pending task before re-raising.

unmatched_peer.body: The `test_streaming` test fetches a third output message (line 503) and then asserts a `TimeoutError` on a fourth (lines 504-505). For a two-chunk streaming response (`first\n` and `last\n`), the ASGI protocol sends: `http.response.start`, `http.response.body` (first chunk), `http.response.body` (last chunk, `more_body=False`). That's only 3 messages total. The third `receive_output` on line 503 should be the final `http.response.body` with `more_body=False`, and the fourth call should indeed time out. This is fine, but the comment "Fetch the rest of the response so that coroutines are cleaned up" is slightly misleading — it would be clearer to assert the type/body of this third message to confirm it's the terminal chunk.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The test silently discards the third output without asserting its content, making it harder to diagnose failures. Minor readability/robustness concern.

unmatched_peer.body:
`functools._lru_cache_wrapper` is a private/internal CPython implementation detail. It is not part of the public API and could be renamed, removed, or changed in future Python versions without notice.

A more robust approach would be to obtain the type dynamically from a known `lru_cache`-wrapped function, e.g.:
```python
_lru_cache_wrapper_type = type(functools.lru_cache(lambda: None))
```
or check for the `__wrapped__` attribute combined with `cache_info` in the serializer logic. Alternatively, `functools.cache` is just `lru_cache(maxsize=None)`, so both are covered by `_lru_cache_wrapper` — but the private name is the concern.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The type `functools._lru_cache_wrapper` is prefixed with an underscore, indicating it is a private implementation detail of the `functools` module. While it has been stable in CPython for a long time, relying on it in Django's public migration serializer registry creates a fragile dependency on CPython internals that could break on alternative Python implementations (e.g., PyPy) or future CPython versions.

unmatched_peer.body: When `error_messages=None`, `self.error_messages` is assigned the class-level `default_error_messages` dict directly (not a copy). This means any mutation of `self.error_messages` on an instance would silently modify the shared class attribute, affecting all future `Paginator` instances. Even if the current code doesn't mutate it, this is a fragile contract. The `error_messages is None` branch should also produce a copy.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `else` branch correctly creates a new dict via `self.default_error_messages | error_messages`, but the `if` branch returns the mutable class-level dict by reference. Any code that does `paginator.error_messages['invalid_page'] = '...'` after construction would corrupt `Paginator.default_error_messages` for all subsequent instances.
unmatched_peer.suggestion:

            self.default_error_messages.copy()
            if error_messages is None
            else self.default_error_messages | error_messages
        )
